t.1.57.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: There was a king named Uparicara, a lord of the earth ever devoted to dharma and firm in his vows. Once he went out to hunt.
t.1.57.2: That lord of the earth, Vasu, the delight of the Pauravas, on Indra's instruction took possession of the lovely land of Cedi, a realm well worth the taking.
t.1.57.3: To that lord of the earth, who had laid down his weapons and was dwelling in a hermitage, devoted to austerities, the god himself, the wielder of the thunderbolt, came in person.
t.1.57.4: Reflecting, "This king, through his austerity, is worthy of the rank of Indra," he himself, in person, turned the king back from his austerity with conciliatory words.
t.1.57.5: Let this dharma not be thrown into confusion upon the earth, O lord of the earth; protect it, for dharma, when upheld, sustains the whole world.
t.1.57.6: Ever devoted and composed, protect the dharma that sustains the world; then, joined with dharma, you will attain the eternal worlds of merit.
t.1.57.7: Dwelling on earth, become the dear friend of me who dwell in heaven, and settle, O lord of men, in that region which is the udder of the earth.
t.1.57.9: For this land surpasses all others, endowed with wealth, jewels and the like, and the earth here is full of riches; dwell among the Cedis, O lord of the Cedis.
t.1.57.8: It is rich in cattle and holy, firmly settled, abounding in wealth and grain, easy to guard and gentle, and endowed with all the enjoyable qualities of a land.
t.1.57.10: The people of the land are virtuous by nature, well contented and good; there is no lying here even among the wanton, so how could there be otherwise?
t.1.57.11: There, men devoted to the welfare of their elders are not separated from their fathers; they do not yoke lean cattle to the pole, but nourish them back to strength.
t.1.57.12: Among the Cedis, O giver of honor, all the varṇas always abide by their own dharma. There is nothing in the three worlds that is unknown to you.
t.1.57.14: You alone among all mortals, mounted upon an excellent celestial chariot, shall move about stationed on high, like a god possessed of bodily form.
t.1.57.13: A great crystal aerial chariot, divine and fit for the enjoyment of the gods, given by me, will come to you in the sky, so that you may range through the heavens.
t.1.57.15: I give you the Vaijayantī garland of unfading lotuses, which will keep you unwounded by weapons in battle.
t.1.57.16: And this very thing shall be your emblem here, O lord of men, renowned as the Garland of Indra, auspicious, incomparable and great.
t.1.57.17: And the slayer of Vṛtra gave him a staff of bamboo as a gift of his favour, a staff that protects the virtuous.
t.1.57.18: Then, when a year had passed, the lord of the earth had it set into the ground for the worship of Śakra.
t.1.57.19: From that time on, even to this day, O king, the bringing in of the pole is performed by the best of kings, just as it was instituted by him.
t.1.57.20: And likewise, on the following day, the kings carry out the raising of the pole, adorned with baskets, perfumes, garlands and ornaments; and, wreathed with strings of garlands, it is duly set up according to the rite.
t.1.57.21: And here the blessed Śaṃkara is worshipped in a laughing form, which he himself assumed out of affection for the great-souled Vasu.
t.1.57.23: Those men and kings who will honor my festival and joyfully cause it to be celebrated, as the king, the lord of the Cedis, does,
t.1.57.22: But the mighty great Indra, O lord, seeing this auspicious worship performed by Vasu, the foremost of kings, was pleased and spoke.
t.1.57.24: Prosperity and victory shall belong to them together with their kingdoms, and likewise the country shall be flourishing and joyful.
t.1.57.25: Thus, O lord of men, was the great king Vasu honored with affection by that great-souled Mahendra, Maghavan.
t.1.57.26: Those men who shall always cause the festival of Śakra to be celebrated, just as they are purified by gifts such as the gift of land, by the granting of boons and by great sacrifices, so too shall they be purified by Śakra's festival.
t.1.57.27: Then Vasu, lord of the Cedis, highly honored by Maghavan, dwelling among the Cedis, ruled this earth with righteousness. Out of love for Indra, King Vasu instituted the festival of Indra.
t.1.57.28: And he had five sons of great valor and boundless energy; and that emperor had his sons consecrated as kings over various kingdoms.
t.1.57.29: There was the great chariot-warrior Bṛhadratha, renowned as the king of Magadha; Pratyagraha; Kuśāmba, whom they called Maṇivāhana; Macchilla; Yadu; and Rājanya, the unconquered.
t.1.57.30: These sons of that royal sage, O king, were of abundant splendor; they established countries and cities called by their own names. They were the five Vāsava kings, and their separate lineages were everlasting.
t.1.57.32: Once, they say, the mountain Kolāhala, endowed with consciousness and moved by desire, blocked the river Śuktimatī that flowed past his city.
t.1.57.31: As he dwelt in a palace like Indra's, high in the crystal sky, the Gandharvas and Apsarases waited upon that great-souled king. And so his name became renowned as King Uparicara, the one who moves above.
t.1.57.33: Then Vasu struck that mountain Kolāhala with his foot, and through the opening made by that blow the river flowed out.
t.1.57.35: The one who was born there a male, him Vasu, that best of royal seers, the giver of wealth, made his general, a tamer of foes; but the maiden Girikā the king made his beloved wife.
t.1.57.34: On that river the mountain himself begot a pair of twins. Pleased at being set free, the river presented them to the king.
t.1.57.36: But Vasu's wife Girikā, out of desire, at the proper time informed him that her season had arrived, having bathed and become pure for the rite of conceiving a son.
t.1.57.37: On that day the ancestors, pleased, then said to him, that best of kings, foremost among the wise: "Kill the deer."
t.1.57.38: Not transgressing that command of the ancestors, the king went hunting, full of desire, thinking only of Girikā, who was exceedingly endowed with beauty, like another Śrī in visible form.
t.1.57.39: As he wandered in the lovely forest, his seed spilled forth; and the moment that seed had fallen, the king caught it with the leaf of a tree.
t.1.57.41: Having thus reflected, the king then pondered it again and again, and that best of kings, knowing that his seed was not to be wasted,
t.1.57.40: The lord caught it, thinking, “Let my semen not be spilled in vain, and let the season of my wife not be fruitless.”
t.1.57.42: Having considered that it was the time for sending the semen to his queen, he consecrated that semen with mantras; then he, who knew the true essence of subtle dharma and artha, recognizing a swift hawk perched nearby, spoke to it.
t.1.57.43: For my sake, gentle one, carry this seed of mine to my house and give it quickly to Girikā, for today is surely her season.
t.1.57.44: Then the swift hawk, seizing it, quickly flew up, and summoning his utmost speed, that bird sped away through the sky.
t.1.57.45: Then another hawk saw that hawk approaching, and the moment he saw him, he swooped upon him at once, suspecting that he carried meat.
t.1.57.46: Then the two of them began a beak-fight in the sky, and as they fought, the semen fell, and it fell into the waters of the Yamunā.
t.1.57.47: There, a choice Apsaras renowned as Adrikā, having taken on the form of a fish through a Brahmin's curse, came to dwell in the Yamunā.
t.1.57.48: Then Adrikā, who had taken the form of a fish, swiftly approached and seized that seed of Vasu, which had fallen from the hawk's feet.
t.1.57.49: Then one day fishermen caught that fish, and when the tenth month had arrived, O best of the Bharatas, they drew out from her belly a human pair, a girl and a boy.
t.1.57.50: Thinking it a marvel, they reported it to the king: "O king, these two human beings have been born in the body of a fish."
t.1.57.51: Of the two, King Uparicara then took the male child; he became a king named Matsya, righteous and true to his promise.
t.1.57.53: Then she, having given birth to the two, was cut open by the fisherman; and that excellent Apsaras, abandoning her fish form and attaining a divine form, went to the path of the Siddhas, Ṛṣis and Cāraṇas.
t.1.57.52: In an instant that apsaras was freed from her curse, she to whom the Lord had once said, while she dwelt in an animal's womb: "O lovely one, after giving birth to two human beings you will obtain release from the curse."
t.1.57.55: But she, Satyavatī by name, the brightly smiling one, for some time smelled of fish because she lived in the company of fishermen.
t.1.57.54: The maiden who was the daughter of that she-fish, and who smelled of fish, was then given by the king to the fisherman with the words, “Let her be yours.” She was endowed with beauty and goodness and rich in every virtue.
t.1.57.56: While wandering on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, Parāśara saw her as she plied a boat on the water in service to her father.
t.1.57.57: As soon as he saw her, exceedingly endowed with beauty, desired even by the Siddhas, lovely to behold, the wise one desired her; the bull among sages, knowing her to be the maiden born of Vasu and having a purpose to fulfil, longed for her.
t.1.57.58: She said, "Look, blessed one, at the seers standing on the near and far banks; while we two are being watched by them, how could our union take place?"
t.1.57.59: Thus addressed by her, the blessed lord created a mist, by which that whole region became as if covered in darkness.
t.1.57.60: Then, seeing the mist created by the supreme seer, the wise maiden, astonished and abashed, spoke to him.
t.1.57.61: Know me, blessed one, to be a maiden, ever subject to my father's will; and through union with you my maidenhood would be defiled, O sinless one.
t.1.57.63: To her, who had spoken thus, the best of sages, well pleased, said: "Having done what is dear to me, you shall remain a maiden still."
t.1.57.62: And if my maidenhood is defiled, how shall I be able to go home, O best of the twice-born? And I could not bear to remain at home, O wise one. Having considered this, O blessed one, arrange what should come next.
t.1.57.65: Thus addressed, she chose as her boon the most excellent fragrance of the body; and the blessed lord granted her that which her heart desired.
t.1.57.64: Choose a boon, timid one, whatever you desire, beautiful lady, for never before has my favor been in vain, O bright-smiling one.
t.1.57.66: Then, having obtained her boons, delighted and adorned with the virtues of womanhood, she entered into union with the seer of wondrous deeds.
t.1.57.67: Therefore her name became famed on earth as Gandhavatī, for men on earth could smell her fragrance from a yojana away.
t.1.57.68: Thereafter her name became renowned as Yojanagandhā, and the blessed Parāśara, for his part, went to his own dwelling.
t.1.57.69: Thus Satyavatī, delighted at having obtained the unsurpassed boon, united with Parāśara and at once brought forth the child; and on an island in the Yamunā was born that mighty son of Parāśara.
t.1.57.70: Having attended upon his mother, he set his mind on austerity alone, and he said, "When I am thought of, I shall appear whenever there are tasks to be done."
t.1.57.71: Thus Dvaipāyana was born of Satyavatī from Parāśara. Because he was placed on an island as a child, he therefore became Dvaipāyana.
t.1.57.72: But he, knowing that dharma loses one quarter in each successive yuga, and having observed that the lifespan and strength of mortals follow the course of the yuga,
t.1.57.74: He taught the Vedas, with the Mahābhārata as the fifth, to Sumantu, Jaimini, Paila, and also to Śuka, his own son.
t.1.57.73: Because, out of a desire to show favor to Brahmā and likewise to the brahmins, he divided the Vedas, he is therefore remembered as Vyāsa.
t.1.57.76: Likewise Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, of boundless splendor, was born in Gaṅgā from the seed of a Vasu, he of great valor and great fame.
t.1.57.75: The mighty lord, most excellent and bestower of boons, taught Vaiśaṃpāyana as well; and by them the saṃhitās of the Bhārata were made known, each separately.
t.1.57.77: An ancient seer, no thief, was impaled on a stake on suspicion of being a thief; he was renowned as Aṇīmāṇḍavya, a man of very great fame.
t.1.57.78: Long ago that great seer summoned Dharma and said this: "In my childhood I pierced a single little bird with a reed."
t.1.57.80: Since the killing of a brahmin is graver than the killing of all other beings, therefore, because of this sin, you shall be born in the womb of a śūdra.
t.1.57.79: I remember that offense, O Dharma; I remember no other sin. Why then did my austerity, a thousandfold greater, not overcome it here?
t.1.57.82: Saṃjaya, the sūta, who was like a sage, was born of Gavalgaṇa; and of Sūrya, in the maiden Kuntī, was born Karṇa, the great chariot-warrior, wearing the armour he was born with, his face lit up by his earrings.
t.1.57.81: Because of that curse, Dharma too was born from a śūdra womb, as the learned Vidura, righteous, embodied, and free from sin.
t.1.57.83: For the sake of showing grace to the worlds, Viṣṇu, revered by the world, the greatly glorious one, became manifest from Vasudeva in Devakī.
t.1.57.84: That god, without beginning or end, is the maker and lord of the world; he is the unmanifest, imperishable Brahman, the primordial source, whose nature is free of qualities.
t.1.57.86: They call him the infinite, the immovable god, the Haṃsa, Nārāyaṇa, the lord, the creator, ageless, eternal, the supreme, the imperishable.
t.1.57.85: Him they know as the imperishable Self, as Prakṛti, the supreme source, as Puruṣa, Viśvakarman, the maker of all, as the union with sattva, the steadfast Imperishable.
t.1.57.87: That Person, the all-pervading Lord, the Creator, the grandsire of all beings, was born among the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis for the sake of increasing dharma.
t.1.57.88: Sātyaki and Kṛtavarman, both knowers of divine weapons, of great valor, skilled in all arms, and devoted followers of Nārāyaṇa, were born of Satyaka and of Hṛdika, the two masters of weaponry.
t.1.57.89: The seed of Bharadvāja, the great seer of fierce austerity, fell and grew in a wooden vessel, and from it Droṇa was born.
t.1.57.91: In the same way Dhṛṣṭadyumna too, radiant as fire itself, was born from the fire when the sacrificial rite was being performed, a mighty hero born together with his bow for the destruction of Droṇa.
t.1.57.90: From Gautama Śaradvat, out of a clump of reeds, twins were born: the mother of Aśvatthāman, and Kṛpa of great strength. Then from Droṇa was born Aśvatthāman, the best of those who bear weapons.
t.1.57.92: In the same way, Kṛṣṇā too was born from the altar, radiant and auspicious, shining with her body and bearing a supreme beauty.
t.1.57.93: Prahrāda's disciple, Nagnajit, then became Subala; his offspring, a destroyer of dharma, was born out of the gods' wrath.
t.1.57.94: The son of the king of Gāndhāra was Śakuni Saubala, and likewise the mother of Duryodhana; both were born knowing the ways of worldly gain.
t.1.57.95: From Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, in the field of Vicitravīrya, was born Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, and also Pāṇḍu of great strength.
t.1.57.96: From Pāṇḍu, by his two wives, were born five sons, each equal to the gods; of them Yudhiṣṭhira was the eldest and foremost in virtues.
t.1.57.97: From Dharma was born Yudhiṣṭhira, and from Māruta, Vṛkodara; from Indra was born the glorious Dhanaṃjaya, the best of all who bear weapons.
t.1.57.98: From the two Aśvins, moreover, were born the twins, both endowed with beauty, Nakula and Sahadeva, devoted to the service of their elders.
t.1.57.100: Abhimanyu was born of Arjuna in Subhadrā, the sister's son of Vāsudeva and the grandson of the great-souled Pāṇḍu.
t.1.57.99: Thus a hundred sons were born to the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana and the others, and likewise Yuyutsu, the Karaṇa.
t.1.57.101: From the five Pāṇḍavas, too, five sons were born in Kṛṣṇā, princes endowed with beauty and skilled in all weapons.
t.1.57.102: Prativindhya was born of Yudhiṣṭhira, Sutasoma of Vṛkodara, Śrutakīrti of Arjuna, and Śatānīka was the son of Nakula.
t.1.57.103: Likewise, from Sahadeva was born the valiant Śrutasena; and in the forest Ghaṭotkaca was born to Hiḍimbā by Bhīma.
t.1.57.104: Śikhaṇḍin was born of Drupada, a maiden who attained the state of a son; the Yakṣa Sthūṇa made her a man out of a wish to do her a kindness.
t.1.57.105: Then, in that war of the Kurus, many hundreds of thousands of kings assembled, intent on fighting in battle.
t.1.57.106: Their names, in every respect, are beyond measure; they cannot be counted even in tens of thousands of years. But these that have been named are the chief ones, by whom this tale has been spread forth.
